title: Curated dinosaur + broader Amniota context tree for museum-style educational app
scope_note: Major dinosaur clades plus a broader Amniota context tree that includes synapsids/mammaliaforms, living and fossil reptiles, pterosaurs, croc-line archosaurs, turtles, lepidosaurs, and selected Mesozoic marine reptiles. The dinosaur clade backbone remains curated from peer-reviewed phylogenetic literature. The expanded non-dinosaur catalog is a museum-prototype seed layer that must be reconciled against PBDB and primary taxonomic descriptions before label-level publication.

display_guidance.museum_safe_claim: An interactive, curator-review-ready tree showing dinosaurs in their broader amniote context, with uncertainty labels for debated relationships.
display_guidance.avoid_claim: Avoid saying this is the complete final tree of all reptiles, mammals, pterosaurs, and dinosaurs.
recommended_ui: Use color bands for Synapsida, Sauropsida/Reptilia, Archosauria, Dinosauria, Pterosauria, Crocodylomorpha, Lepidosauria, Testudinata, and Marine Reptiles.
Show pterosaurs as close relatives of dinosaurs on the avian-line archosaur branch, not as dinosaurs.
Show crocodylians/crocodylomorphs as the living/extinct crocodile-line archosaurs, not dinosaur descendants.
Show mammals on the synapsid branch, as the sister deep branch to reptiles within Amniota.

Use warning badges for fossil groups whose exact placement is debated, especially early amniotes, early mammaliaforms, turtles in fossil-only datasets, ichthyosaurs, sauropterygians, and mosasauroid basal relationships.

topology_policy.reason: The split into Ornithischia and Saurischia remains a familiar and still widely used educational scaffold, but the deep relationships among Ornithischia, Theropoda and Sauropodomorpha are actively debated.
topology_policy.deep_tree_warning: Recent analyses and reviews find no settled consensus at the base of Dinosauria; major alternatives include Ornithoscelida and hypotheses involving silesaurids close to or within Ornithischia.

species_catalog_policy.scope: non-avian dinosaur species where possible, with a small flagged avialan/stem-context set for educational continuity
species_catalog_policy.recommended_public_claim: Includes a broad, curated starter catalog of dinosaur species/taxa, with PBDB reconciliation fields and uncertainty flags.
species_catalog_policy.avoid_public_claim: Complete list of all dinosaur species or final authoritative placement for every species.
species_catalog_policy.why_not_complete: New species are published continually; synonymy, nomina dubia, and placements change; living birds would add more than ten thousand dinosaur species if crown birds are included.
museum_publish_requirements: Run PBDB taxon-name reconciliation and keep PBDB identifiers in each species record.
Separate valid species, nomina dubia, synonyms, nomina nuda, and non-dinosaur/stem taxa.
Attach original description or revision references for any species shown in a museum label.
Use expert review for debated taxa and for all deep-tree placements.

nodes.label: Amniota
nodes.status_note: Egg/embryo adaptations unite mammals and reptiles including birds. The deepest split is between Synapsida and Sauropsida, but early fossil timing and some Paleozoic placements remain actively studied.

nodes.label: Synapsida
nodes.status_note: Mammal-line amniotes, including mammals and their extinct stem relatives such as non-mammalian synapsids.

nodes.label: Non-mammalian synapsids
nodes.status_note: Educational grade for extinct stem mammals outside Mammaliaformes; do not display as a formal monophyletic clade unless subdivided.

nodes.label: Therapsida
nodes.status_note: Major synapsid radiation including dicynodonts, gorgonopsians, therocephalians, cynodonts, and mammals.

nodes.label: Cynodontia
nodes.status_note: Includes mammals and many close extinct mammal relatives.

nodes.label: Mammaliaformes
nodes.status_note: Includes Mammalia and close fossil relatives; specialized Mesozoic groups can move depending on character partition and analysis.

nodes.label: Docodonta
nodes.status_note: Extinct mammaliaforms with diverse Jurassic-Cretaceous ecologies; exact relationship to other mammaliaforms can vary across datasets.

nodes.label: Eutriconodonta
nodes.status_note: Extinct Mesozoic mammaliaform group including relatively large predators such as Repenomamus.

nodes.label: Haramiyida
nodes.status_note: Placement is debated and can affect the inferred age/composition of crown Mammalia.

nodes.label: Multituberculata
nodes.status_note: Long-lived extinct mammal-like clade; placement relative to crown mammals has varied in analyses.

nodes.label: Mammalia
nodes.rank_or_level: crown or near-crown mammal clade depending definition
nodes.status_note: Crown mammals include monotremes and therian mammals; exact fossil membership near the crown boundary is debated.

nodes.label: Monotremata
nodes.status_note: Egg-laying mammals, represented today by platypus and echidnas; fossil relatives often discussed within australosphenidan debates.

nodes.label: Theria
nodes.status_note: Live-bearing mammal clade including marsupials and placentals.

nodes.label: Metatheria
nodes.status_note: Marsupial-line therians.

nodes.label: Eutheria
nodes.status_note: Placental-line therians; early fossil placement can be controversial.

nodes.label: Sauropsida / Reptilia
nodes.status_note: Reptile-line amniotes, including living reptiles and birds plus many extinct groups.

nodes.label: Early sauropsids and stem reptiles
nodes.status_note: Educational grade for early reptile-line amniotes; many Paleozoic placements are debated.

nodes.label: Diapsida
nodes.status_note: Major reptile clade including lepidosaurs, archosauromorphs, and many extinct marine reptiles.

nodes.label: Lepidosauromorpha
nodes.status_note: Includes lepidosaurs and possibly some extinct marine reptile relationships depending on analysis.

nodes.label: Lepidosauria
nodes.status_note: Tuatara plus squamates: lizards, snakes, amphisbaenians, and extinct close relatives.

nodes.label: Rhynchocephalia
nodes.status_note: Tuatara lineage and extinct relatives.

nodes.label: Squamata
nodes.status_note: Lizards, snakes, amphisbaenians, and extinct mosasaurs.

nodes.label: Mosasauroidea
nodes.status_note: Marine lizard relatives of the Late Cretaceous; basal relationships and origins of aquatic adaptations remain studied.

nodes.label: Archelosauria
nodes.status_note: Groups turtles with archosaurs in many molecular datasets; fossil-only placement of turtles has historically been difficult and should be labelled carefully.

nodes.label: Testudinata / turtle total group
nodes.status_note: Turtle total group including fossil stem turtles and crown Testudines; exact early stem placement remains debated.

nodes.label: Testudines
nodes.status_note: Living turtle crown group and close fossil members.

nodes.label: Archosauromorpha
nodes.status_note: Reptile branch containing archosaurs and their stem relatives.

nodes.label: Archosauriformes
nodes.status_note: Includes archosaurs and several Triassic stem groups.

nodes.label: Archosauria
nodes.status_note: Crown group split into crocodile-line pseudosuchians and bird-line avemetatarsalians.

nodes.label: Pseudosuchia / crocodile-line archosaurs
nodes.status_note: Crocodile-line archosaurs including living crocodylians and many extinct Triassic/Mesozoic forms.

nodes.label: Aetosauria
nodes.status_note: Armored Triassic pseudosuchians, not dinosaurs.

nodes.label: Rauisuchian-grade pseudosuchians
nodes.status_note: Useful educational grouping for large Triassic croc-line predators; avoid presenting as a single secure clade without caveat.

nodes.label: Crocodylomorpha
nodes.status_note: Includes living crocodiles/alligators/caimans/gharials and their extinct relatives; many fossil species were terrestrial, marine, or herbivorous/omnivorous, unlike the modern stereotype.

nodes.label: Crocodyliformes
nodes.status_note: More crownward crocodylomorphs including notosuchians, marine thalattosuchians, neosuchians, and crocodylians.

nodes.label: Notosuchia
nodes.status_note: Mostly Gondwanan terrestrial crocodyliforms with high ecological diversity.

nodes.label: Thalattosuchia
nodes.status_note: Marine crocodylomorphs; not dinosaurs and not direct ancestors of modern crocodiles.

nodes.label: Neosuchia
nodes.status_note: Includes many semi-aquatic crocodyliforms and crown Crocodylia.

nodes.label: Crocodylia
nodes.status_note: Living crocodiles, alligators, caimans, gharials, and their crown relatives.

nodes.label: Avemetatarsalia / bird-line archosaurs
nodes.status_note: Bird-line archosaurs including pterosaurs and dinosaurs.

nodes.label: Pterosauromorpha
nodes.status_note: Pterosaur total-group concept; often includes lagerpetids as closest known pterosaur relatives in recent work.

nodes.label: Lagerpetidae
nodes.status_note: Cursorial Triassic relatives that help bridge the anatomical gap to pterosaurs; placement as pterosaur sister group is currently influential but should be labelled with source.

nodes.label: Pterosauria
nodes.status_note: First vertebrates known to evolve powered flight. Pterosaurs are close relatives of dinosaurs but are not dinosaurs.

nodes.label: Non-pterodactyloid pterosaurs
nodes.status_note: Educational grade for many early long-tailed pterosaurs; avoid presenting as a formal exclusive clade.

nodes.label: Monofenestrata
nodes.status_note: Pterosaurs with confluent external naris and antorbital fenestra, including wukongopterids and pterodactyloids.

nodes.label: Pterodactyloidea
nodes.status_note: Mostly short-tailed Jurassic-Cretaceous pterosaurs including many famous large and crested forms.

nodes.label: Ornithocheiriformes
nodes.status_note: Large-toothed and related pterodactyloids; exact family-level taxonomy can be revised.

nodes.label: Azhdarchoidea
nodes.status_note: Includes tapejarids and azhdarchids in many analyses; relationships among subgroups vary.

nodes.label: Dinosauromorpha
nodes.status_note: Dinosaur-line archosaurs including dinosaurs and some close Triassic relatives.

nodes.label: Mesozoic marine reptiles
nodes.status_note: Useful display category only. Ichthyosaurs, sauropterygians, mosasaurs, and marine crocodylomorphs are separate lineages that independently adapted to aquatic life.

nodes.label: Ichthyosauromorpha / Ichthyopterygia
nodes.status_note: Fully marine Mesozoic reptiles with uncertain deeper placement among diapsids; treat as marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.

nodes.label: Ichthyosauria
nodes.status_note: Classic ichthyosaurs, many with streamlined bodies, flippers, live birth, and pelagic adaptations.

nodes.label: Sauropterygia
nodes.status_note: Diverse Mesozoic marine reptiles including placodonts, pachypleurosaurs, nothosaurs, pistosaurs, and plesiosaurs; deeper diapsid affinities vary among studies.

nodes.label: Placodontia
nodes.status_note: Triassic marine reptiles, many with crushing teeth and sometimes turtle-like armor.

nodes.label: Eosauropterygia
nodes.status_note: Includes pachypleurosaurs, nothosaurs, pistosaurs, and plesiosaur line.

nodes.label: Plesiosauria
nodes.status_note: Long-lived Jurassic-Cretaceous marine reptiles, traditionally divided into plesiosauromorph and pliosauromorph body forms; not dinosaurs.

nodes.label: Dinosauria
nodes.status_note: Dinosaurs include non-avian dinosaurs and birds. Deep internal relationships are debated. In this broader file Dinosauria is nested inside Dinosauromorpha within bird-line archosaurs.

nodes.label: Ornithischia
nodes.status_note: A major herbivorous dinosaur radiation. Its exact position relative to Theropoda and Sauropodomorpha is debated in recent higher-level analyses.

nodes.label: Heterodontosauridae
nodes.status_note: Often treated as early-diverging ornithischians, but early ornithischian topology remains sensitive to taxon and character sampling.

nodes.label: Thyreophora
nodes.status_note: Armoured ornithischians, including stegosaurs and ankylosaurs.

nodes.label: Stegosauria
nodes.status_note: Plated/spiked armoured dinosaurs. Internal relationships vary between analyses.

nodes.label: Ankylosauria
nodes.status_note: Armoured dinosaurs traditionally divided into nodosaurid and ankylosaurid lineages.

nodes.label: Nodosauridae
nodes.status_note: One of the two traditional main ankylosaurian branches.

nodes.label: Ankylosauridae
nodes.status_note: One of the two traditional main ankylosaurian branches; many members have tail clubs.

nodes.label: Neornithischia
nodes.status_note: Broad clade containing ornithopods and marginocephalians, with early branching relationships still debated.

nodes.label: Ornithopoda
nodes.status_note: Includes small bipedal forms and large iguanodontians/hadrosaurs; exact early membership is revised in recent analyses.

nodes.label: Iguanodontia
nodes.status_note: Derived ornithopods including iguanodontians and hadrosaur-line taxa.

nodes.label: Hadrosauroidea
nodes.status_note: Hadrosaur-line ornithopods, including duck-billed dinosaurs.

nodes.label: Marginocephalia
nodes.status_note: Commonly used clade uniting pachycephalosaurs and ceratopsians; some early ornithischian relationships remain sensitive.

nodes.label: Pachycephalosauria
nodes.status_note: Dome-headed ornithischians; fossil record is mostly Cretaceous and relationships are affected by incomplete material.

nodes.label: Ceratopsia
nodes.status_note: Horned/frilled ornithischians and their relatives, from basal forms to ceratopsids.

nodes.label: Neoceratopsia
nodes.status_note: More derived ceratopsians including protoceratopsids and ceratopsids.

nodes.label: Ceratopsidae
nodes.status_note: Large Late Cretaceous horned dinosaurs; commonly split into centrosaurine and chasmosaurine lineages.

nodes.label: Saurischia
nodes.rank_or_level: major dinosaur clade in traditional topology
nodes.status_note: Traditional grouping of Theropoda + Sauropodomorpha; challenged by Ornithoscelida and other recent hypotheses.

nodes.label: Sauropodomorpha
nodes.rank_or_level: major saurischian clade in traditional topology
nodes.status_note: Long-necked herbivorous lineage including sauropods; position relative to Theropoda and Ornithischia is part of the deep Dinosauria debate.

nodes.label: Plateosauria / early sauropodomorph grade
nodes.status_note: Use carefully: early sauropodomorph taxonomy has changed; this node is useful for education but should be curated against a specific phylogenetic matrix before publication.

nodes.label: Sauropoda
nodes.status_note: Giant, mostly quadrupedal long-necked dinosaurs.

nodes.label: Eusauropoda
nodes.status_note: Derived sauropod clade forming the core of classic sauropod diversity.

nodes.label: Neosauropoda
nodes.status_note: Usually divided into Diplodocoidea and Macronaria.

nodes.label: Diplodocoidea
nodes.status_note: Peg-toothed neosauropods including diplodocids, dicraeosaurids and rebbachisaurids.

nodes.label: Macronaria
nodes.status_note: Neosauropods including camarasaurids, brachiosaurids and titanosaurs.

nodes.label: Titanosauriformes
nodes.status_note: Includes brachiosaurids and titanosaurs; internal relationships can change with new material.

nodes.label: Titanosauria
nodes.status_note: Highly diverse Cretaceous sauropods; internal relationships are often unstable.

nodes.label: Theropoda
nodes.rank_or_level: major saurischian clade in traditional topology
nodes.status_note: Mostly carnivorous bipedal dinosaurs; includes birds. Its deep relationship to Ornithischia/Sauropodomorpha is debated.

nodes.label: Neotheropoda
nodes.status_note: Includes coelophysoids and more derived theropods.

nodes.label: Coelophysoidea
nodes.status_note: Early-diverging neotheropods; exact early theropod topology can vary.

nodes.label: Averostra
nodes.status_note: Clade including Ceratosauria and Tetanurae.

nodes.label: Ceratosauria
nodes.status_note: Theropod clade including ceratosaurs and abelisauroids.

nodes.label: Tetanurae
nodes.status_note: Major theropod clade including megalosauroids, allosauroids, coelurosaurs and birds.

nodes.label: Megalosauroidea
nodes.status_note: Basal tetanuran radiation including megalosaurids and spinosaurids; relationships differ among analyses.

nodes.label: Avetheropoda
nodes.status_note: Commonly used grouping including allosauroids and coelurosaurs.

nodes.label: Allosauroidea
nodes.status_note: Large-bodied theropods including allosaurids, carcharodontosaurids and relatives.

nodes.label: Coelurosauria
nodes.status_note: Theropod clade including tyrannosauroids, ornithomimosaurs, maniraptorans and birds.

nodes.label: Tyrannosauroidea
nodes.status_note: Tyrannosaur-line coelurosaurs, from small basal forms to large tyrannosaurids.

nodes.label: Maniraptoriformes
nodes.status_note: Includes ornithomimosaurs and maniraptorans.

nodes.label: Ornithomimosauria
nodes.status_note: Ostrich-like coelurosaurs.

nodes.label: Maniraptora
nodes.status_note: Includes oviraptorosaurs, therizinosaurs, paravians and birds.

nodes.label: Oviraptorosauria
nodes.status_note: Beaked maniraptorans; exact position relative to other maniraptorans varies.

nodes.label: Therizinosauria
nodes.status_note: Herbivorous/omnivorous maniraptorans with unusual forelimbs and claws.

nodes.label: Paraves
nodes.status_note: Includes dromaeosaurids, troodontids and avialans; internal topology is debated.

nodes.label: Dromaeosauridae
nodes.status_note: Raptor dinosaurs. Internal dromaeosaurid relationships and some taxa vary among analyses.

nodes.label: Troodontidae
nodes.status_note: Traditionally grouped with dromaeosaurids as deinonychosaurs, but paravian relationships are debated.

nodes.label: Avialae
nodes.status_note: Bird-line dinosaurs; basal membership and exact positions near Archaeopteryx are debated.

alternative_topologies.label: Ornithoscelida hypothesis
alternative_topologies.summary: Places Ornithischia and Theropoda as sister clades, with Sauropodomorpha outside that pairing; proposed by Baron et al. and supported under additional criteria by Parry et al., but challenged by Langer et al. and subsequent work.

alternative_topologies.label: Traditional Saurischia + Ornithischia scaffold
alternative_topologies.summary: Places Ornithischia as sister to Saurischia, with Saurischia containing Sauropodomorpha and Theropoda. Still common in teaching and display, but not settled as the exclusive best-supported root topology.

alternative_topologies.label: Silesaurid / stem-ornithischian hypotheses
alternative_topologies.summary: Some recent analyses place traditionally non-dinosaurian silesaurids close to or within the ornithischian stem, potentially helping explain the poor Triassic ornithischian body-fossil record. Treat as an advanced optional layer, not the default childrenâ€™s/museum basic display.

alternative_topologies.label: Broad Amniota context scaffold
alternative_topologies.summary: Places dinosaurs inside Dinosauromorpha/Avemetatarsalia/Archosauria/Sauropsida, pterosaurs as close non-dinosaur relatives on the pterosaur branch, crocodile-line archosaurs as Pseudosuchia, and mammals as Synapsida outside Sauropsida.

alternative_topologies.label: Marine reptiles are an ecological category, not one clade
alternative_topologies.summary: Ichthyosaurs, sauropterygians, mosasaurs, and marine crocodylomorphs are separate reptile lineages that independently adapted to marine life. The UI may group them visually as an exhibit theme, but the phylogenetic tree should not show them as one natural clade.

uncertain_or_wildcard_taxa.label: Herrerasauridae
uncertain_or_wildcard_taxa.status_note: Important early carnivorous dinosaur-lineage group. Placement varies: sometimes near Theropoda, sometimes outside Theropoda, and relevant to the deep Saurischia/Ornithoscelida debate.

uncertain_or_wildcard_taxa.label: Chilesaurus
uncertain_or_wildcard_taxa.status_note: Problematic Jurassic taxon whose position has been interpreted in different ways; useful as an uncertainty case study rather than a fixed node in the public scaffold.

uncertain_or_wildcard_taxa.label: Silesauridae / silesaurids
uncertain_or_wildcard_taxa.status_note: Dinosauriforms with contested relevance to early ornithischian origins; include only with explicit uncertainty labels.

important_filters: Decide whether Avialae/crown birds are in scope. For a non-avian dinosaur app, exclude crown birds and usually separate Mesozoic avialans.

Check taxon_status, accepted_name, senior synonyms, and reference records before public display.
Store PBDB taxon_no/reference_no/occurrence_no rather than copying unreviewed long labels into museum panels.

data_integration_notes.pbdb: Use PBDB for occurrence records, stratigraphic intervals, localities, and bibliographic links. Do not use PBDB alone to infer phylogenetic parent-child relationships.
data_integration_notes.opentree: Use Open Tree of Life as a cross-reference/taxonomy reconciliation aid. Do not treat all OpenTree paths as peer-reviewed phylogenetic support unless the supporting sources are checked.
data_integration_notes.timetree: Use mainly for living bird divergence-time context. It is not a primary source for extinct non-avian dinosaur divergence times.

context_tree_policy.important_public_explanation: Dinosaurs, pterosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, lizards/snakes, and mammals are all amniotes. Mammals are synapsids. Dinosaurs, birds, crocodiles, pterosaurs, turtles, lizards/snakes, and most extinct marine reptiles are sauropsids/reptiles. Pterosaurs are not dinosaurs; they are close relatives on the avian-line archosaur side. Crocodiles are not dinosaurs; they are crocodile-line archosaurs.
context_tree_policy.museum_caution: This file is a scaffold plus species/taxon seed catalog, not a complete all-species phylogeny. Use PBDB and primary literature to verify each taxon before public museum label use.

educational_panels.title: Are pterosaurs dinosaurs?
educational_panels.short_answer: No. Pterosaurs are flying reptiles close to dinosaurs on the bird-line archosaur branch, but they are outside Dinosauria.
educational_panels.recommended_display: Place Pterosauria beside Dinosauromorpha/Dinosauria under Avemetatarsalia, not inside Dinosauria.

educational_panels.title: Are crocodiles dinosaurs?
educational_panels.short_answer: No. Crocodiles and dinosaurs are both archosaurs, but crocodiles belong to the crocodile-line branch Pseudosuchia while dinosaurs belong to the bird-line branch.
educational_panels.recommended_display: Place Crocodylomorpha under Pseudosuchia as the sister-side branch to Avemetatarsalia.

educational_panels.title: Where do mammals fit?
educational_panels.short_answer: Mammals are synapsid amniotes. They are outside the reptile-line branch that contains dinosaurs, pterosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, lizards, snakes, and birds.
educational_panels.recommended_display: Show Mammaliaformes under Synapsida as the deep sister branch to Sauropsida/Reptilia within Amniota.

educational_panels.title: Are all marine reptiles related to each other?
educational_panels.short_answer: No. â€œMarine reptilesâ€ is an ecological exhibit category, not a single natural clade. Ichthyosaurs, sauropterygians, mosasaurs, and marine crocodylomorphs adapted to water independently.
educational_panels.recommended_display: Use a separate thematic filter for marine reptiles, but keep them on their separate branches in the phylogenetic tree.

educational_panels.title: Are birds dinosaurs?
educational_panels.short_answer: Yes. Birds are living theropod dinosaurs and should remain nested inside Dinosauria.
educational_panels.recommended_display: Keep Avialae/Aves inside Theropoda/Maniraptora, not as an external branch next to dinosaurs.
